## Where we are going

By week 4 you will make a humanoid walk using nothing but geometry and physics
you derived yourself.

From week 7 on you will replace hand-written control with policies the robot
learns on its own (weeks 8–10 train them, week 12 makes one survive pushes).

Today: why simulation, and how to drive one — the file that describes a robot
(**MJCF**), the arrays it compiles into (`qpos`, `qvel`), and the loop that
moves it forward in time (the **integrator**), including the one way it fails.

This is **Layers 1 and 2** of the week-0 stack: the physics engine and the
robot model.

---

## Colour code for the week {.smaller}

The same colours mean the same things in every equation and every drawing:

| symbol | meaning | in MuJoCo | colour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}$ | **position**: joint angles, and where the base is | `data.qpos` | <span style="color:#3b7dd8">blue</span> |
| ${\color{#2a9d5c}{v = \dot q}}$ | **velocity**: how fast each of those is changing | `data.qvel` | <span style="color:#2a9d5c">green</span> |
| ${\color{#e8743b}{\tau,\ F}}$ | a **torque** (on a hinge) or a **force** (on a body) | `qfrc_*` | <span style="color:#e8743b">orange</span> |
| ${\color{#c0392b}{h}}$ | the **timestep**: how far one step jumps in time | `model.opt.timestep` | <span style="color:#c0392b">red</span> |
| ${\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}$ | a spring's **natural frequency**: how fast it would oscillate, rad/s | — | <span style="color:#8e44ad">purple</span> |

Plain letters are constants you can read off the model: $m$ a mass (kg),
$k$ a stiffness (N/m, or N·m/rad for a hinge — the servo gain `kp` is one),
$g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\zeta$ ("zeta") a damping ratio. A subscript $n$
is the step number, so ${\color{#3b7dd8}{q_n}}$ is the position after $n$ steps.

---

## Why simulate a robot at all?

A real humanoid is expensive, fragile, and slow to reset.

- A fall costs money and repair time
- Experiments must be repeatable to be science
- Learning needs **millions** of trials — impossible on hardware
- Simulation runs faster than real time, and in parallel

This course is **simulation only**. Everything you build runs on your laptop or
in Colab.

---

## The cost of simulating

Simulation is an approximation, and the places it is wrong are the places robots
fall over:

- Contact and friction are *hard* — the foot/ground interface is the whole game
- Actuators have limits, delays, and heat that models ignore
- Sensors are noiseless in sim and never noiseless in reality

The distance between simulation and reality is the **sim-to-real gap**. We return
to it in week 12.

---

## MuJoCo

**Mu**lti-**Jo**int dynamics with **Co**ntact — a physics engine built for exactly
our problem: many joints, and contact with the ground.

- Free and open source
- Fast enough for reinforcement learning
- Strong contact model, which is why locomotion research uses it

```bash
pip install mujoco
```

---

## MJCF: a robot is a text file

MuJoCo reads **MJCF**, an XML format. One file describes an entire robot, and
each top-level section answers a different question about it.

```xml
<mujoco model="my_robot">
  <compiler angle="radian" meshdir="assets"/>    <!-- how to read this file   -->
  <option timestep="0.002" gravity="0 0 -9.81"/> <!-- how the world behaves   -->
  <default>   ...  </default>                    <!-- values tags inherit     -->
  <asset>     ...  </asset>                      <!-- meshes, materials       -->
  <worldbody> ...  </worldbody>                  <!-- the robot: bodies       -->
  <actuator>  ...  </actuator>                   <!-- what you can command    -->
  <sensor>    ...  </sensor>                     <!-- what you can measure    -->
  <keyframe>  ...  </keyframe>                   <!-- named poses             -->
</mujoco>
```

A file with nothing but `<worldbody>` compiles happily. The other seven sections
are the difference between a shape and a robot.

---

## Body, joint, geom {.smaller}

Three tags carry almost all the meaning.

```xml
<body name="upper_leg" pos="0 0 1">                            <!-- frame + mass -->
  <joint name="hip" type="hinge" axis="0 1 0"/>                <!-- how it moves -->
  <geom type="capsule" size="0.05" fromto="0 0 0  0 0 -0.4"/>  <!-- its shape    -->

  <body name="lower_leg" pos="0 0 -0.4">                       <!-- a child link -->
    <joint name="knee" type="hinge" axis="0 1 0"/>
    <geom type="capsule" size="0.04" fromto="0 0 0  0 0 -0.4"/>
  </body>
</body>
```

- **`<body>`** — a coordinate frame carrying mass. `pos` is measured **from its
  parent**, not from the world — which is why moving the thigh moves the shin
  with it, and why you never recompute a child's position by hand.
- **`<joint>`** — how this body may move *relative to its parent*. A body with no
  joint is welded to its parent and adds no freedom.
- **`<geom>`** — shape: what you see, and what collides.

Nesting `<body>` **is** the kinematic chain — rotate the hip and the shin comes
with it, because its frame is defined inside the thigh's. Week 2 makes this
precise.

code runs locally and on Colab.

```{python}
import mujoco
import soc4180

soc4180.set_seed(4180)
print("GL backend:", soc4180.GL_BACKEND, "| Colab:", soc4180.is_colab())

model = soc4180.load_g1()   # fetches the pinned G1 on first use, then caches it
data = mujoco.MjData(model)
```

## What is in the model? {.smaller}

Three numbers describe the robot's size as a dynamical system.

```{python}
print(f"nq    = {model.nq:3d}   generalised coordinates (position)")
print(f"nv    = {model.nv:3d}   degrees of freedom (velocity)")
print(f"nu    = {model.nu:3d}   actuators (motors you can command)")
print(f"nbody = {model.nbody:3d}   rigid bodies")
```

**`nq` is larger than `nv`.** The floating base uses a 4-number quaternion for
orientation but has only 3 rotational DOF. A free-floating robot is not a fixed
robot arm, and that difference drives everything about balance.

---

## Which way is up? {.smaller}

Before any joint name makes sense, you need the frame those names live in.

```{python}
print("gravity     :", model.opt.gravity)
for side in ("left", "right"):
    b = mujoco.mj_name2id(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_BODY, f"{side}_hip_pitch_link")
    print(f"{side:5s} hip at:", model.body_pos[b])
```

- **`+z` is up** — gravity points along $-z$.
- **`+y` is the robot's left** — the left hip sits at $y = +0.064$ m, the right at
  $y = -0.064$ m.
- **`+x` is forward.** You do not have to take that on faith: the frame is
  right-handed, and $x = y \times z$, so left-cross-up gives forward.

Lengths are **metres** and angles are **radians** — `<compiler angle="radian"/>`
said so. The `1.28` you saw in the `stand` keyframe is an elbow bent 73°.

---

## Roll, pitch, and yaw {.smaller}

Three words for turning about the three axes. Try them with your own head:

| Name | Turns about | Your head | The robot |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **roll** | `x` — forward | tilt an ear toward your shoulder | tipping sideways |
| **pitch** | `y` — left | nod "yes" | leaning forward or back |
| **yaw** | `z` — up | shake "no" | turning to face a new direction |

The G1's joint names are not decoration — each one *is* its axis:

```{python}
for n in ["left_hip_pitch_joint", "left_hip_roll_joint", "left_hip_yaw_joint",
          "left_knee_joint", "left_ankle_pitch_joint", "left_ankle_roll_joint"]:
    j = mujoco.mj_name2id(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_JOINT, n)
    print(f"{n:24s} axis {model.jnt_axis[j]}")
```

Check it across the whole robot — every named hinge agrees with its axis:

```{python}
axis_name = {(1, 0, 0): "roll", (0, 1, 0): "pitch", (0, 0, 1): "yaw"}
mismatch = []
for j in range(model.njnt):
    n = mujoco.mj_id2name(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_JOINT, j)
    if not n or model.jnt_type[j] != mujoco.mjtJoint.mjJNT_HINGE:
        continue
    got = axis_name.get(tuple(int(round(v)) for v in model.jnt_axis[j]))
    for word in ("roll", "pitch", "yaw"):
        if word in n and got != word:
            mismatch.append((n, got))
print("joints whose name disagrees with their axis:", mismatch or "none")
```

---

## Why a hip needs three and a knee needs one {.smaller}

The hip is **three separate joints stacked** — `hip_pitch`, `hip_roll`,
`hip_yaw` — because a leg must do three independent things:

- **pitch** — swing forward to take a step
- **roll** — spread sideways, and shift weight onto one foot
- **yaw** — turn the leg so the robot can change direction

The knee has only **pitch**: `left_knee_joint` has axis `[0 1 0]`, and its range
is `[-0.087, 2.880]` — it bends one way and essentially does not straighten past
zero. Yours is the same. That single-axis, one-sided knee is why week 3's inverse
kinematics has a reachable set with a *hole* in the middle.

Three notes you will need later:

- Two of these are easy to sense and one is not. An accelerometer feels gravity,
  so it can tell you **roll and pitch** — but gravity says nothing about which
  way you are *facing*, so **yaw is unobservable** from it. Week 6.
- Rotations do not commute: roll-then-pitch is not pitch-then-roll. This is why
  week 2 uses matrices and quaternions rather than three angles.
- The floating base stores its orientation as the quaternion `(w, x, y, z)` —
  **scalar first**, which is MuJoCo's convention and not everyone's.

## The file you actually loaded {.smaller}

`load_g1()` compiled a real file that is sitting on this machine. Here it is, in
full — the *scene*, which is not the robot.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

scene_xml = soc4180.robot_path("unitree_g1", "scene")
print(scene_xml, end="\n\n")
print(Path(scene_xml).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
```

Twenty lines: a floor, a sky, a light — and `<include file="g1.xml"/>`, which
pulls in the robot. **The robot and its world are separate files**, so the same
G1 can be dropped onto a different floor without editing the robot.

## Reading the robot's own file {.smaller}

`g1.xml` is 350 lines, so we print it one section at a time.

```{python}
def mjcf(path, tag, limit=40):
    """Print one top-level block of an MJCF file: <tag> ... </tag>."""
    lines = Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
    i = next(k for k, l in enumerate(lines) if l.lstrip().startswith(f"<{tag}"))
    if lines[i].rstrip().endswith("/>"):          # self-closing, e.g. <option .../>
        return print(lines[i].strip())
    pad = len(lines[i]) - len(lines[i].lstrip())  # close the tag at *this* depth
    j = next(k for k, l in enumerate(lines[i:], i)
             if l.lstrip().startswith(f"</{tag}") and len(l) - len(l.lstrip()) == pad)
    block = lines[i:j + 1]
    extra = len(block) - limit
    print("\n".join(block[:limit] + ([f"  ... {extra} more lines"] if extra > 0 else [])))

g1_xml = soc4180.robot_path("unitree_g1", "g1")
mjcf(g1_xml, "compiler")
mjcf(g1_xml, "option")
```

`angle="radian"` sets the units of every angle in the file. `meshdir` says where
the STL files live.

---

## What the file does not say {.smaller}

That `<option>` line sets an integrator and nothing else. Yet the simulation
plainly has a timestep and a gravity vector:

```{python}
print(f"timestep = {model.opt.timestep} s  ->  {1/model.opt.timestep:.0f} Hz")
print(f"gravity  = {model.opt.gravity}")
```

Those are **MuJoCo's defaults**, not the model's choices. An MJCF is a *diff
against a default robot*: every attribute you leave out still has a value.

That cuts both ways. It keeps files short — and it means a number you never
wrote is shaping your results.

---

## `<default>`: where `kp=500` comes from {.smaller}

Search the G1's 29 actuator lines for a gain and you will not find one.

```{python}
mjcf(g1_xml, "default")
```

`<default class="g1">` names a bundle of attributes. The pelvis carries
`childclass="g1"`, so every tag beneath it inherits them, and any tag can opt
into a class by name — `class="visual"`, `class="collision"`, `class="foot"`.

**This is where the position gain of 500 that runs your whole semester lives.**
Classes nest: `foot` inherits from `collision`, which inherits from `g1`.

---

## One link, in full {.smaller}

```{python}
mjcf(g1_xml, "body", limit=13)
```

Everything a link can carry, in one place:

- `pos="0 0 0.793"` — the pelvis starts 79 cm above the floor
- `<inertial>` — mass and rotational inertia: the numbers the physics integrates
- `<freejoint>` — this body may translate and rotate freely: it is **not** bolted
  to the world
- `<geom class="visual">` twice, `class="collision"` once — one link, drawn one
  way and collided another
- `<site>` — a named point carrying no physics; sensors mount here
- then a nested `<body>`, where the left leg begins

---

## Nesting is the kinematic chain {.smaller}

The compiled model remembers the tree that the XML indentation drew.

```{python}
def tree(m, body=0, depth=0, maxdepth=2):
    name = mujoco.mj_id2name(m, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_BODY, body) or "world"
    print("    " * depth + name)
    if depth == maxdepth:
        return
    for b in range(m.nbody):
        if m.body_parentid[b] == body and b != body:
            tree(m, b, depth + 1, maxdepth)

tree(model, maxdepth=3)
print(f"\n{model.nbody} bodies in total")
```

One root (`pelvis`) and three branches: two legs, and a waist carrying torso,
head and arms.

---

## The G1's tree, drawn {.smaller}

The same `body_parentid` array, drawn instead of printed. Every line is one
parent → child link, and every child hangs on its parent by exactly one joint.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

par = model.body_parentid
kids = {b: [c for c in range(1, model.nbody) if par[c] == b] for b in range(model.nbody)}
row, depth = {}, {0: 0}
def place(b, slot=[0]):
    """Each chain's tip gets its own row; a parent sits level with the middle of its children."""
    for c in kids[b]:
        depth[c] = depth[b] + 1
        place(c)
    if kids[b]:
        row[b] = np.mean([row[c] for c in kids[b]])
    else:
        row[b] = slot[0]; slot[0] += 1
place(0)

def chain_colour(b):
    n = mujoco.mj_id2name(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_BODY, b) or "world"
    if "left" in n and ("hip" in n or "knee" in n or "ankle" in n):  return "#3b7dd8"
    if "right" in n and ("hip" in n or "knee" in n or "ankle" in n): return "#2a9d5c"
    if "left" in n:  return "#8e44ad"
    if "right" in n: return "#e8743b"
    return "0.35"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.6))
for b in range(1, model.nbody):
    ax.plot([depth[par[b]], depth[b]], [-row[par[b]], -row[b]], color="0.75", lw=1.2, zorder=1)
for b in range(model.nbody):
    n = (mujoco.mj_id2name(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_BODY, b) or "world")
    short = n.replace("_link", "").replace("left_", "L ").replace("right_", "R ")
    ax.scatter(depth[b], -row[b], s=45, color=chain_colour(b), zorder=2)
    ax.text(depth[b] - 0.05, -row[b] + 0.12, short, rotation=30, ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlim(-0.4, max(depth.values()) + 1.3); ax.set_ylim(-max(row.values()) - 0.4, 1.0); ax.axis("off")
ax.set_title("the G1's body tree, root on the left: blue left leg, green right leg, "
             "purple left arm, orange right arm, grey trunk", fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("deepest body:", mujoco.mj_id2name(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_BODY, max(depth, key=depth.get)),
      "at depth", max(depth.values()))
```

Read it left to right: `world` → `pelvis` (through the free joint) → five
chains. **A body's position depends only on the joints on its path to the
root** — the path from a hand back up passes through the waist and never
through a leg, which is why a knee cannot move a hand. Week 2b measures exactly
that.

---

## Every link is drawn twice {.smaller}

```{python}
import numpy as np
from collections import Counter

groups = Counter(int(g) for g in model.geom_group)
non_colliding = sum((model.geom_contype[i] == 0) and (model.geom_conaffinity[i] == 0)
                    for i in range(model.ngeom))
print("geoms by group :", dict(sorted(groups.items())))
print("non-colliding  :", non_colliding, f"of {model.ngeom}")

foot = mujoco.mj_name2id(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_BODY, "left_ankle_roll_link")
for g in range(model.ngeom):
    if model.geom_bodyid[g] == foot:
        print(f"  foot geom: group {model.geom_group[g]}  "
              f"type {mujoco.mjtGeom(model.geom_type[g]).name:14s} "
              f"collides={bool(model.geom_contype[g])}")
```

Group 2 is the pretty mesh, declared `contype="0" conaffinity="0"` — **invisible
to physics**. Group 3 is what actually touches the world.

The foot reaches the ground through **four spheres of 5 mm radius**, not a mesh.
Sphere contacts are cheap and stable; mesh-on-mesh contact is neither. Choices
like this one are what keep a 29-joint humanoid fast enough to learn in.

---

## Joints decide `nq` and `nv` {.smaller}

The joint type you write determines how many numbers the state needs.

```{python}
def dof_count(joint_xml):
    xml = f"""<mujoco><worldbody><body pos="0 0 1">{joint_xml}
              <geom type="box" size=".1 .1 .1"/></body></worldbody></mujoco>"""
    m = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string(xml)
    return m.nq, m.nv

for label, tag in [("<freejoint/>",      "<freejoint/>"),
                   ('type="ball"',       '<joint type="ball"/>'),
                   ('type="slide"',      '<joint type="slide" axis="0 0 1"/>'),
                   ('type="hinge"',      '<joint type="hinge" axis="0 1 0"/>'),
                   ("no joint (welded)", "")]:
    nq, nv = dof_count(tag)
    print(f"{label:20s} nq={nq}  nv={nv}")
```

`freejoint` and `ball` are the only rows where **`nq` exceeds `nv`**: both store
orientation as a 4-number quaternion for 3 real freedoms.

The G1 is one `freejoint` plus 29 hinges — `nq` = 7 + 29 = 36, `nv` = 6 + 29 = 35.
The gap you met a few slides ago is now fully explained.

---

## `qpos` and `qvel`, drawn {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
fj = 0                                           # joint 0 is the free joint
print("free joint : qpos", model.jnt_qposadr[fj], "..", model.jnt_qposadr[fj] + 6,
      "| qvel", model.jnt_dofadr[fj], "..", model.jnt_dofadr[fj] + 5)
kn = mujoco.mj_name2id(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_JOINT, "left_knee_joint")
print("left knee  : qpos", model.jnt_qposadr[kn], "| qvel", model.jnt_dofadr[kn])

segs_q = [("base\nx y z", 3, "#3b7dd8"), ("base quaternion\nw x y z", 4, "#8e44ad"),
          ("left leg", 6, "0.55"), ("right leg", 6, "0.7"), ("waist", 3, "0.55"),
          ("left arm", 7, "0.7"), ("right arm", 7, "0.55")]
segs_v = [("base\nlinear", 3, "#2a9d5c"), ("base\nangular", 3, "#8e44ad")] + segs_q[2:]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 2.7))
for row, segs, label in ((1, segs_q, f"qpos ({model.nq})"), (0, segs_v, f"qvel ({model.nv})")):
    x = 0
    for name, n, col in segs:
        for i in range(n):
            ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x + i, row), 0.95, 0.6, color=col, alpha=0.85))
        ax.text(x + n / 2, row + 0.75 if row else row - 0.25, name, ha="center",
                va="bottom" if row else "top", fontsize=7.5)
        x += n
    ax.text(-0.6, row + 0.3, label, ha="right", va="center", fontsize=9, weight="bold")
qa, da = model.jnt_qposadr[kn], model.jnt_dofadr[kn]
ax.annotate("", xy=(da + 0.47, 0.62), xytext=(qa + 0.47, 0.98), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#c0392b", lw=1.8))
ax.text(qa + 1.4, 0.8, f"left knee: qpos[{qa}] ↔ qvel[{da}]", color="#c0392b", fontsize=8, va="center")
ax.set_xlim(-6, 37); ax.set_ylim(-0.9, 2.2); ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

- **Top row, `qpos`:** 3 numbers say *where* the pelvis is (metres), 4 say *how
  it is turned* (a quaternion), then one angle per hinge (radians).
- **Bottom row, `qvel`:** 3 for how fast the pelvis moves, but only **3** for how
  fast it turns (an angular velocity, rad/s), then one rate per hinge.
- Because the base spends one more number in `qpos`, **every hinge sits one slot
  further along in `qpos` than in `qvel`** (the red arrow). Always look addresses
  up with `jnt_qposadr` and `jnt_dofadr`; never reuse one index on the other array.

---

## Four numbers for three turns: the quaternion {.smaller}

A turn by angle $\theta$ about a unit axis $\mathbf{n}$ is stored as

$$\mathbf{u} = (w,\ x,\ y,\ z) = \big(\cos\tfrac{\theta}{2},\ \ \mathbf{n}\,\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\big),
\qquad w^2 + x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1 .$$

- $\mathbf{n}$ — the axis you turn about (3 numbers, length 1); $\theta$ — how far, in radians
- the **scalar $w$ comes first** in MuJoCo; `(1, 0, 0, 0)` means "not turned"
- the length-1 rule is **one constraint on four numbers**, leaving **3 freedoms** — so `nv` counts 3

Why not three angles? Three angles have a pose where two of them do the same
thing and a freedom disappears (week 2 measures it). Four numbers with one rule
never do. And why only 3 numbers in `qvel`? A velocity lives in the directions
you can actually move — the angular velocity ${\color{#2a9d5c}{\boldsymbol\omega}}$,
3 numbers, rad/s.

That means the integrator cannot do "quaternion + $h$ × velocity" — the sizes do
not even match. It **turns** the quaternion instead, by angle
$h\,|{\color{#2a9d5c}{\boldsymbol\omega}}|$ about ${\color{#2a9d5c}{\boldsymbol\omega}}$, every step. Test it:
spin a free box at 1 rad/s about $z$ for 1 s, with gravity off.

```{python}
BOX = """<mujoco><option gravity="0 0 0"/><worldbody><body>
         <freejoint/><geom type="box" size=".1 .2 .3"/></body></worldbody></mujoco>"""
box = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string(BOX)
db = mujoco.MjData(box)
db.qvel[3:6] = [0, 0, 1.0]                 # angular velocity: 1 rad/s about z
while db.time < 1.0 - 1e-9:
    mujoco.mj_step(box, db)
print("quaternion after 1 s :", np.round(db.qpos[3:7], 6))
print("cos(1/2), sin(1/2)   :", round(np.cos(0.5), 6), round(np.sin(0.5), 6))
print("length |u| - 1       :", f"{np.linalg.norm(db.qpos[3:7]) - 1:.1e}")
```

One radian about $z$ gives exactly $(\cos\frac12, 0, 0, \sin\frac12)$, and the
quaternion is still length 1 after 500 steps.

---

## Actuators live outside the body tree {.smaller}

```{python}
mjcf(g1_xml, "actuator", limit=6)
```

A `<position>` actuator is a **servo**: you command an angle and an internal loop
with gain `kp` produces the torque. Note what is *not* written — the limits.

```{python}
a = mujoco.mj_name2id(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_ACTUATOR, "left_knee_joint")
j = mujoco.mj_name2id(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_JOINT, "left_knee_joint")
print("joint range   :", np.round(model.jnt_range[j], 4))
print("ctrl range    :", np.round(model.actuator_ctrlrange[a], 4))
print("position gain :", model.actuator_gainprm[a][0])
```

`inheritrange="1"` in the class copied the joint's range onto the actuator, so a
command outside the joint's travel cannot even be expressed. The gain came from
the class too.

**29 actuators for 35 degrees of freedom.** The missing six are the floating
base: nothing pushes the robot around except the floor.

---

## Sensors attach to sites {.smaller}

```{python}
mjcf(g1_xml, "sensor")
```

Every sensor names a `<site>` — the frame it measures in. Move that site in the
XML and the readings change, exactly as remounting the real IMU would.

Note what is **absent**: no camera, no foot contact switch, no joint-torque
sensor. A robot cannot sense what its file does not declare. The `noise` and
`cutoff` attributes are a week-6 topic.

---

## Keyframes: named poses {.smaller}

```{python}
mjcf(g1_xml, "keyframe")

key = model.key_qpos[0]
print("\nposition   :", key[:3])
print("quaternion :", key[3:7], " (w, x, y, z — scalar first)")
names = [mujoco.mj_id2name(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_JOINT, i) for i in range(model.njnt)]
bent = {n: float(key[model.jnt_qposadr[i]])
        for i, n in enumerate(names)
        if n != "floating_base_joint" and key[model.jnt_qposadr[i]]}
print("non-zero joints:", bent)
```

Those 36 numbers are exactly `qpos`: 3 for position, 4 for the quaternion, 29 for
the joints. `<key>` sets `ctrl` too, so the servos are told to hold the pose the
robot starts in.

Only the arms are bent. **Every leg joint is exactly zero** — perfectly straight
legs. It looks tidy, and it is a trap: week 4 shows why inverse kinematics cannot
escape it.

---

## XML in, arrays out {.smaller}

The compiler flattens the tree into arrays. Learning this mapping is most of what
"knowing MuJoCo" means:

| In the file | In `model` |
| --- | --- |
| `<body pos="...">` | `body_pos`, `body_parentid`, `body_mass` |
| `<joint type=... range=...>` | `jnt_type`, `jnt_range`, `jnt_qposadr` |
| `<geom class="collision">` | `geom_type`, `geom_group`, `geom_contype` |
| `<position kp="500">` | `actuator_gainprm`, `actuator_ctrlrange` |
| `<site>` | `site_pos`, and `data.site_xpos` once kinematics runs |
| `<key qpos="...">` | `key_qpos`, `key_ctrl` |
| `<option>` and defaults | `model.opt` |

Names are optional in MJCF — the G1's foot spheres have none — but ids always
exist. `mj_name2id` and `mj_id2name` cross between the two worlds.

---

## Now write one yourself {.smaller}

A robot, from nothing, in twenty lines.

```{python}
LEG = """
<mujoco model="two_link_leg">
  <option timestep="0.002"/>
  <worldbody>
    <light pos="0 0 3" dir="0 0 -1" directional="true"/>
    <geom name="floor" type="plane" size="5 5 0.05" rgba="0.3 0.4 0.5 1"/>

    <body name="upper_leg" pos="0 0 1">
      <joint name="hip" type="hinge" axis="0 1 0"/>
      <geom type="capsule" size="0.05" fromto="0 0 0  0 0 -0.4" rgba="0.7 0.7 0.7 1"/>

      <body name="lower_leg" pos="0 0 -0.4">
        <joint name="knee" type="hinge" axis="0 1 0"/>
        <geom type="capsule" size="0.04" fromto="0 0 0  0 0 -0.4" rgba="0.2 0.2 0.2 1"/>
      </body>
    </body>
  </worldbody>

  <actuator>
    <position name="hip"  joint="hip"  kp="200" dampratio="1"/>
    <position name="knee" joint="knee" kp="200" dampratio="1"/>
  </actuator>
</mujoco>
"""

leg = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string(LEG)
print(f"nq={leg.nq}  nv={leg.nv}  nu={leg.nu}  nbody={leg.nbody}  ngeom={leg.ngeom}")
```

Two hinges, so `nq = nv = 2`. `nbody` is 3 because the world itself counts as a
body. There is no `<freejoint>`, so the hip is bolted to the sky: this leg cannot
fall over, only swing.

---

## Frames: every `pos` is measured from the parent {.smaller}

Each `<body>` is a **frame** — an origin plus three axes — and its `pos` is
written in its parent's frame. Bend the hip 1.2 rad and the knee −0.8 rad (the
pose the next slide holds) and let MuJoCo place everything:

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
pose = np.array([1.2, -0.8])
dl = mujoco.MjData(leg); dl.qpos[:] = pose
mujoco.mj_forward(leg, dl)                 # joint angles -> every frame in world coordinates

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.8, 4.2))
ax.axhline(0, color="0.3", lw=2)
for b, col in ((0, "0.3"), (1, "#3b7dd8"), (2, "#2a9d5c")):
    o, R = dl.xpos[b], dl.xmat[b].reshape(3, 3)
    for axis, c in ((0, "#c0392b"), (2, "#3b7dd8")):         # x axis red, z axis blue
        tip = o + 0.18 * R[:, axis]
        ax.annotate("", xy=(tip[0], tip[2]), xytext=(o[0], o[2]),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=1.8, color=c))
    ax.plot(o[0], o[2], "o", color=col, ms=8, zorder=3)
    if b:
        end = o + R @ np.array([0, 0, -0.4])                 # the capsule, in the body's own frame
        ax.plot([o[0], end[0]], [o[2], end[2]], lw=9, color=col, alpha=0.35, solid_capstyle="round")
names = ["world  (0, 0, 0)", "upper_leg  pos = 0 0 1\n(in world)", "lower_leg  pos = 0 0 -0.4\n(in upper_leg's frame)"]
for b, txt in enumerate(names):
    left = b == 2                                            # keep the shin's label off the thigh
    ax.text(dl.xpos[b][0] + (-0.06 if left else 0.05), dl.xpos[b][2] + (0.1 if b == 1 else 0.05), txt, fontsize=8.5,
            ha="right" if left else "left")
ax.set_xlim(-1.25, 0.65); ax.set_ylim(-0.1, 1.3); ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_xlabel("x (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("z (m)"); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.set_title("each body's frame: red = its x axis, blue = its z axis (the hinges turn about y, into the page)", fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The shin's `pos` never changed — it is still `0 0 -0.4` — but the thigh's frame
turned, so the knee landed somewhere else. Positive rotation about $+y$ swings
a downward leg towards $-x$: the right-hand rule, thumb along $+y$ (into the
page here).

---

## Frames: the rule, checked {.smaller}

$${\color{#3b7dd8}{\mathbf{p}_{\text{child}}}} = \mathbf{p}_{\text{parent}} + R_{\text{parent}}\;\mathbf{pos}_{\text{child}}$$

- $\mathbf{p}$ — a frame's origin in **world** coordinates (`data.xpos`)
- $R_{\text{parent}}$ — the parent frame's 3×3 rotation, its axes as columns (`data.xmat`)
- $\mathbf{pos}_{\text{child}}$ — the number you typed in the XML (`model.body_pos`)

Read it as: start at the parent's origin, then walk the typed offset *along the
parent's own axes*, wherever they now point. Check it against MuJoCo for the
pose on the last slide:

```{python}
R_up = dl.xmat[1].reshape(3, 3)
predicted = dl.xpos[1] + R_up @ leg.body_pos[2]
print("lower_leg origin, from MuJoCo            :", np.round(dl.xpos[2], 4))
print("parent origin + R_parent @ pos, by hand   :", np.round(predicted, 4))
print("difference                                :", f"{np.abs(predicted - dl.xpos[2]).max():.1e} m")
```

Exactly zero: this is how MuJoCo places every child's origin (orientations
compose the same way). Apply it from the root outwards and you have every body
in the robot — week 2 builds it into forward kinematics.

---

## Your robot, servos on and off {.smaller}

Start it bent, and ask the servos to **hold that bent pose** — a pose gravity
would never choose.

```{python}
TARGET = np.array([1.2, -0.8])          # the pose drawn on the last slide

data_leg = mujoco.MjData(leg)
data_leg.qpos[:] = TARGET
data_leg.ctrl[:] = TARGET               # servos: stay exactly where you are
servo = soc4180.render_rollout(leg, data_leg, duration=3.0, fps=30, width=480, height=360)
print("servos on :", np.round(data_leg.qpos, 3), " droop:", np.round(data_leg.qpos - TARGET, 3))
data_leg_servo_q = data_leg.qpos.copy()   # kept for the next slide

data_leg = mujoco.MjData(leg)
data_leg.qpos[:] = TARGET
with soc4180.actuation_disabled(leg):
    passive = soc4180.render_rollout(leg, data_leg, duration=3.0, fps=30,
                                     width=480, height=360)
print("no actuation:", np.round(data_leg.qpos, 3))

soc4180.show_video(servo, fps=30)
soc4180.show_video(passive, fps=30)
```

Same file, same start, same gravity. The first is a machine holding a pose; the
second is a double pendulum. **The difference is entirely `<actuator>`** — the
week-0 lesson, in a model you wrote yourself.

It does not hold *perfectly*: the hip sags a few hundredths of a radian. A
proportional servo only makes torque when it is already wrong, so gravity always
wins a little. That residue is where week 5 begins.

---

## The droop, derived {.smaller}

The servo's torque on each joint is a spring plus a damper:

$${\color{#e8743b}{\tau}} = k_p\,(\text{ctrl} - {\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}) - k_v\,{\color{#2a9d5c}{\dot q}}$$

- $k_p$ — stiffness, N·m per radian of error (200 in our file)
- $k_v$ — damping, N·m per rad/s; `dampratio="1"` told the compiler to pick it for us
- $\text{ctrl}$ — the angle you asked for; ${\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}$ the angle it has

**Step 1 — at rest** the velocity is zero, so the damper does nothing:
${\color{#e8743b}{\tau}} = k_p(\text{ctrl} - {\color{#3b7dd8}{q}})$.

**Step 2 — at rest nothing accelerates**, so the servo's torque must exactly
cancel gravity's torque ${\color{#e8743b}{\tau_g}}({\color{#3b7dd8}{q}})$ on that joint:
$k_p(\text{ctrl} - {\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}) = {\color{#e8743b}{\tau_g}}$.

**Step 3 — solve for the error:**
$${\color{#3b7dd8}{q}} - \text{ctrl} = -\,{\color{#e8743b}{\tau_g}} / k_p .$$

**A non-zero load needs a non-zero error.** A proportional servo makes torque
only by being wrong, so to hold up a leg it must stay a little wrong.

---

## The droop, predicted {.smaller}

MuJoCo reports the gravity torque at any pose as `qfrc_bias` (at rest it is
gravity alone), so Step 3 predicts the droop before simulating anything:

```{python}
d0 = mujoco.MjData(leg); d0.qpos[:] = TARGET
mujoco.mj_forward(leg, d0)
kp_leg = leg.actuator_gainprm[:, 0]
print("gravity torque at TARGET  :", np.round(d0.qfrc_bias, 2), "N·m  (hip, knee)")
print("predicted droop  -tau_g/kp :", np.round(-d0.qfrc_bias / kp_leg, 4), "rad")

q = TARGET.copy()                          # Step 3 used tau_g at TARGET; the leg is really at q
for _ in range(20):
    d0.qpos[:] = q; mujoco.mj_forward(leg, d0)
    q = TARGET - d0.qfrc_bias / kp_leg     # re-evaluate gravity where the leg actually is
print("same, with tau_g at the drooped pose:", np.round(q - TARGET, 4), "rad")
print("measured after 3 s (last slide)     :", np.round(data_leg_servo_q - TARGET, 4), "rad")
```

The first guess is a few per cent off because gravity's torque changes as the
leg sags; evaluate it where the leg actually ends up and the prediction agrees
with the simulation. **Nothing in the simulator is magic: the servo equation
and Newton's balance give the number.**

---

## The droop, against the gain {.smaller}

Step 3 says the droop is ${\color{#3b7dd8}{q}} - \text{ctrl} = -{\color{#e8743b}{\tau_g}}/k_p$:
double the gain, halve the error. Test that across a range of gains
(`LEG.replace` edits the XML text, then it is recompiled):

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def droop(kp, seconds=3.0):
    m = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string(LEG.replace('kp="200"', f'kp="{kp}"'))
    d = mujoco.MjData(m); d.qpos[:] = TARGET; d.ctrl[:] = TARGET
    while d.time < seconds:
        mujoco.mj_step(m, d)
    return d.qpos - TARGET

gains = np.array([5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500])
hip = np.array([droop(k)[0] for k in gains])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 3.4))
ax.loglog(gains, -hip, "o-", lw=2, color="#3b7dd8", label="hip droop, measured")
ax.loglog(gains, -hip[-2] * 200 / gains, "--", color="0.5", label=r"$\propto 1/k_p$")
ax.set_xlabel("$k_p$"); ax.set_ylabel("droop below TARGET (rad)"); ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which="both")
ax.set_title("a servo commanded to a pose gravity fights never quite gets there", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("droop at kp=200:", f"{hip[-2]:+.4f} rad;", "at kp=5:", f"{hip[0]:+.3f} rad")
```

Ten times the gain, a tenth of the error — and never zero. Removing the error
entirely needs a term that remembers (an integrator) or one that knows about
gravity in advance (feedforward). Both are week 5.

---

## `model` is the robot; `data` is the moment {.smaller}

You have been using both since the third cell. They are not the same kind of
thing, and confusing them is the most common MuJoCo mistake.

```{python}
print("model  — compiled from the XML, and constant while you simulate")
print(f"   nq={model.nq}  nv={model.nv}  nu={model.nu}   body_pos, jnt_range, actuator_gainprm ...")

d = mujoco.MjData(model)
print("\ndata   — everything that changes")
print(f"   qpos {d.qpos.shape}   joint positions")
print(f"   qvel {d.qvel.shape}   joint velocities")
print(f"   ctrl {d.ctrl.shape}   what you command")
print(f"   xpos {d.xpos.shape}  where every body ended up, in world coordinates")
print(f"   time {d.time}")
```

`model` is the blueprint; `data` is one robot, at one instant, in one universe.

**One `model` can serve many `data`.** That is not a curiosity — it is how week 10
runs thousands of robots at once on a GPU: one description, thousands of moments.

---

## One step of physics {.smaller}

```{python}
d = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand")
print(f"before  t={d.time:.3f}s  pelvis z={d.qpos[2]:.6f}  max |qvel|={np.abs(d.qvel).max():.4f}")

mujoco.mj_step(model, d)

print(f"after   t={d.time:.3f}s  pelvis z={d.qpos[2]:.6f}  max |qvel|={np.abs(d.qvel).max():.4f}")
print(f"\none step advanced time by exactly opt.timestep = {model.opt.timestep} s")
```

Reading it: the clock moved by exactly one timestep, and the pelvis moved
**up** by 0.018 mm — the keyframe starts the feet a hair inside the floor and
the floor is pushing them out (*Watching the floor push back*, below).

That is the whole simulation. Everything else in this course is a decision about
what to write into `data.ctrl` before each step:

```python
while not done:
    data.ctrl[:] = my_controller(data)   # weeks 2-6: maths.  weeks 7-10: a policy.
    mujoco.mj_step(model, data)
```

`mj_step` advances time. Its cousin **`mj_forward`** computes positions from
`qpos` *without* advancing time — that is what draws a pose without letting the
robot fall over, and why `render_poses` exists for the kinematics weeks.

---

## Inside `mj_step`: the equation it solves {.smaller}

Newton's $F = ma$, written for a whole tree of bodies at once, in joint coordinates:

$$M({\color{#3b7dd8}{q}})\;{\color{#2a9d5c}{\dot v}} \;+\; {\color{#e8743b}{c}}({\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}, {\color{#2a9d5c}{v}})
\;=\; {\color{#e8743b}{\tau}} \;+\; {\color{#e8743b}{\tau_{\text{contact}}}}$$

- $M({\color{#3b7dd8}{q}})$ — the **mass matrix**, `nv × nv` (35 × 35): the "$m$" of $F = ma$ for every joint at once. It depends on the pose — a stretched arm is harder to swing than a folded one
- ${\color{#2a9d5c}{\dot v}}$ — the accelerations, `data.qacc`: the unknown
- ${\color{#e8743b}{c}}$ — gravity plus the forces that come from moving (Coriolis, centrifugal), `qfrc_bias`
- ${\color{#e8743b}{\tau}}$ — what the motors push with, `qfrc_actuator` (plus springs in the model, `qfrc_passive`)
- ${\color{#e8743b}{\tau_{\text{contact}}}}$ — the floor and the joint limits pushing back, `qfrc_constraint`

`mj_step` does two things, in order: **(1) solve** this equation for
${\color{#2a9d5c}{\dot v}}$, then **(2) integrate**: use ${\color{#2a9d5c}{\dot v}}$ to jump
${\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}$ and ${\color{#2a9d5c}{v}}$ forward by one timestep ${\color{#c0392b}{h}}$. Check (1) on the standing G1:

```{python}
d = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand")
for _ in range(500):
    mujoco.mj_step(model, d)
mujoco.mj_forward(model, d)                     # recompute every quantity at this state
M = np.zeros((model.nv, model.nv))
mujoco.mj_fullM(model, d, M)                    # the dense 35 x 35 mass matrix
lhs = M @ d.qacc + d.qfrc_bias
rhs = d.qfrc_actuator + d.qfrc_passive + d.qfrc_constraint
print(f"largest term       : {np.abs(rhs).max():8.2f} N or N·m")
print(f"|left - right| max : {np.abs(lhs - rhs).max():8.1e}")
```

Both sides agree to round-off. Everything the simulator "knows" about physics is
in that one line; the rest is how to take step (2) without lying.

---

## One call of `mj_step`, drawn {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.5, 3.3)); ax.axis("off"); ax.set_xlim(0, 10.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 3.3)
boxes = [(0.2, "state\n$q_n,\\ v_n$\n(qpos, qvel)", "#3b7dd8"),
         (2.3, "your controller\nwrites ctrl", "0.45"),
         (4.4, "forces\nactuators, gravity,\ncontacts found", "#e8743b"),
         (6.5, "solve\n$M\\dot v = \\tau - c$\nfor $\\dot v$ (qacc)", "#2a9d5c"),
         (8.6, "integrate\njump by $h$", "#c0392b")]
for x, txt, col in boxes:
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x, 1.3), 1.7, 1.4, boxstyle="round,pad=0.05", fc=col, alpha=0.18, ec=col, lw=1.5))
    ax.text(x + 0.85, 2.0, txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9)
for x in (1.9, 4.0, 6.1, 8.2):
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x + 0.4, 2.0), xytext=(x + 0.05, 2.0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=1.8))
ax.annotate("", xy=(1.05, 1.25), xytext=(9.45, 1.25),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=1.8, color="#c0392b", connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.1"))
ax.text(5.25, 0.25,"$q_{n+1},\\ v_{n+1}$: the new state, time advanced by $h$ = 0.002 s — then repeat",
        ha="center", fontsize=9, color="#c0392b")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The loop on the last slide runs this cycle 500 times per simulated second. The
controller is the only box that is yours; the red arrow is the integrator, and
it is the subject of the next slides.

---

## From a derivative to a step {.smaller}

The integrator turns "how fast things change" into "where things are next".

**Step 1 — the definition of velocity:**
${\color{#2a9d5c}{v}}(t) = \dfrac{d{\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}}{dt} = \lim_{{\color{#c0392b}{h}} \to 0} \dfrac{{\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}(t + {\color{#c0392b}{h}}) - {\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}(t)}{{\color{#c0392b}{h}}}$.

**Step 2 — stop before the limit.** Keep ${\color{#c0392b}{h}}$ small but finite and
rearrange: ${\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}(t + {\color{#c0392b}{h}}) \approx {\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}(t) + {\color{#c0392b}{h}}\,{\color{#2a9d5c}{v}}(t)$.
The same for velocity and acceleration: ${\color{#2a9d5c}{v}}(t + {\color{#c0392b}{h}}) \approx {\color{#2a9d5c}{v}}(t) + {\color{#c0392b}{h}}\,{\color{#2a9d5c}{\dot v}}(t)$.

**Step 3 — count steps instead of seconds** ($t = n{\color{#c0392b}{h}}$):

$${\color{#3b7dd8}{q_{n+1}}} = {\color{#3b7dd8}{q_n}} + {\color{#c0392b}{h}}\,{\color{#2a9d5c}{v_n}},
\qquad
{\color{#2a9d5c}{v_{n+1}}} = {\color{#2a9d5c}{v_n}} + {\color{#c0392b}{h}}\,{\color{#2a9d5c}{\dot v_n}} .$$

This is **explicit (forward) Euler**: everything on the right is already known.

**What it costs.** The exact motion is ${\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}(t+{\color{#c0392b}{h}}) = {\color{#3b7dd8}{q}} + {\color{#c0392b}{h}}{\color{#2a9d5c}{v}} + \tfrac12 {\color{#c0392b}{h}}^2{\color{#2a9d5c}{\dot v}} + \dots$
(Taylor's series). Step 2 dropped the ${\color{#c0392b}{h}}^2$ term, so each step is wrong by about
$\tfrac12{\color{#c0392b}{h}}^2{\color{#2a9d5c}{\dot v}}$; one second takes $1/{\color{#c0392b}{h}}$ steps, so the errors add up to about
$\tfrac12{\color{#c0392b}{h}}\,{\color{#2a9d5c}{\dot v}}$ per second. **Halve the step, halve the error** — that is what
"first-order" means.

---

## MuJoCo's "Euler" is *semi-implicit* {.smaller}

MuJoCo makes one change to Step 3: update the velocity **first**, then move
with the **new** velocity:

$${\color{#2a9d5c}{v_{n+1}}} = {\color{#2a9d5c}{v_n}} + {\color{#c0392b}{h}}\,{\color{#2a9d5c}{\dot v_n}},
\qquad
{\color{#3b7dd8}{q_{n+1}}} = {\color{#3b7dd8}{q_n}} + {\color{#c0392b}{h}}\,{\color{#2a9d5c}{v_{n+1}}} .$$

Check it on a dropped ball, where $\dot v = -g$ exactly. Starting at rest,
${\color{#2a9d5c}{v_n}} = -g{\color{#c0392b}{h}}n$, and adding up $N$ position steps:

- semi-implicit: $z_N = z_0 - g{\color{#c0392b}{h}}^2\,(1 + 2 + \dots + N) = z_0 - g{\color{#c0392b}{h}}^2\,\tfrac{N(N+1)}{2}$
- explicit: the sum stops one term earlier, $z_0 - g{\color{#c0392b}{h}}^2\,\tfrac{N(N-1)}{2}$
- exact: $z_0 - \tfrac12 g\,(N{\color{#c0392b}{h}})^2 = z_0 - g{\color{#c0392b}{h}}^2\,\tfrac{N^2}{2}$

```{python}
BALL = """<mujoco><worldbody><body pos="0 0 10">
          <freejoint/><geom type="sphere" size="0.1"/></body></worldbody></mujoco>"""
ball = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string(BALL); dball = mujoco.MjData(ball)
N, h, g = 500, ball.opt.timestep, 9.81
for _ in range(N):
    mujoco.mj_step(ball, dball)
print(f"MuJoCo after {N} steps : z = {dball.qpos[2]:.5f} m")
print(f"semi-implicit formula : z = {10 - g * h**2 * N * (N + 1) / 2:.5f} m")
print(f"explicit formula      : z = {10 - g * h**2 * N * (N - 1) / 2:.5f} m")
print(f"exact physics         : z = {10 - g * (N * h)**2 / 2:.5f} m")
```

MuJoCo matches the semi-implicit formula to every printed digit. After 1 s
($N = 500$) it is **1 cm** below the exact answer, which is $\tfrac12 g{\color{#c0392b}{h}}\,t$
= ½ × 9.81 × 0.002 × 1 m — the first-order error of the last slide, exactly.
One swapped line looks cosmetic. The next slide shows it is the difference
between a spring that works and one that explodes.

---

## A stiff spring, one step as a matrix {.smaller}

A mass $m$ on a spring of stiffness $k$ — a servo holding a joint is exactly this:

$$m\,\ddot x = -k\,x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \ddot x = -{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}^2 x,
\qquad {\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}} = \sqrt{k/m}\ \ (\mathrm{rad/s}) .$$

**Step 1 — one explicit Euler step is a matrix** acting on the state $(x, v)$:
$$\begin{pmatrix} x_{n+1} \\ v_{n+1} \end{pmatrix} =
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & {\color{#c0392b}{h}} \\ -{\color{#c0392b}{h}}{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}^2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}}_{A}
\begin{pmatrix} x_n \\ v_n \end{pmatrix} .$$

**Step 2 — $n$ steps is $A^n$.** If $A$ has an eigenvalue $\lambda$ with
$|\lambda| > 1$, the state is multiplied by $|\lambda|$ every step and grows
without bound. $|\lambda| \le 1$ for both eigenvalues: it stays bounded.

**Step 3 — the eigenvalues** solve $(1-\lambda)^2 + {\color{#c0392b}{h}}^2{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}^2 = 0$, so
$\lambda = 1 \pm i\,{\color{#c0392b}{h}}{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}$ and

$$|\lambda| = \sqrt{1 + {\color{#c0392b}{h}}^2{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}^2} \;>\; 1 \quad\text{for every } {\color{#c0392b}{h}} > 0 .$$

**Explicit Euler cannot hold an undamped spring at any timestep**: the swing
grows a little every step, for ever. Smaller ${\color{#c0392b}{h}}$ only slows the growth.

---

## The same spring, semi-implicit: $h < 2/\omega$ {.smaller}

**Step 4 — MuJoCo's order.** $v_{n+1} = v_n - {\color{#c0392b}{h}}{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}^2 x_n$, then
$x_{n+1} = x_n + {\color{#c0392b}{h}}\,v_{n+1} = (1 - {\color{#c0392b}{h}}^2{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}^2)\,x_n + {\color{#c0392b}{h}}\,v_n$:

$$A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 - {\color{#c0392b}{h}}^2{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}^2 & {\color{#c0392b}{h}} \\ -{\color{#c0392b}{h}}{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}^2 & 1 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad \det A = 1, \qquad \operatorname{tr} A = 2 - {\color{#c0392b}{h}}^2{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}^2 .$$

**Step 5 — read the eigenvalues off det and trace.** They solve
$\lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr}A)\,\lambda + \det A = 0$, so $\lambda_1\lambda_2 = 1$.

- If $|\operatorname{tr}A| \le 2$ the roots are a complex pair with equal size; their product is 1, so **both have $|\lambda| = 1$**: bounded, for ever.
- If $|\operatorname{tr}A| > 2$ the roots are real with product 1, so **one is bigger than 1**: it explodes.

**Step 6 — solve** $|2 - {\color{#c0392b}{h}}^2{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}^2| \le 2 \iff {\color{#c0392b}{h}}^2{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}^2 \le 4$:

$$\boxed{\;{\color{#c0392b}{h}} \;<\; \frac{2}{{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}} = 2\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}\;}$$

Read it aloud: **the stiffer the spring or the lighter the thing on it, the
smaller the step must be.** Four times the stiffness halves the largest safe
step. A spring's period is $2\pi/{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}$, so the rule says: take more
than $\pi \approx 3$ steps per oscillation, or the simulation cannot see it.

---

## The bound, measured {.smaller}

A 1 kg block on a servo spring with $k = 10\,000$ N/m and no damping:
${\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}} = \sqrt{10\,000/1} = 100$ rad/s, so the bound says
${\color{#c0392b}{h}} < 2/100 = 0.02$ s (the stiffness is chosen so the bound lands on
the lab's broken timestep).

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
def spring(h, integrator="Euler", steps=200):
    xml = f"""<mujoco><option timestep="{h}" gravity="0 0 0" integrator="{integrator}"/>
      <worldbody><body><joint name="x" type="slide" axis="1 0 0"/>
      <inertial pos="0 0 0" mass="1" diaginertia="1 1 1"/></body></worldbody>
      <actuator><position joint="x" kp="10000"/></actuator></mujoco>"""
    m = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string(xml); d = mujoco.MjData(m); d.qpos[0] = 0.01
    xs = [d.qpos[0]]
    for _ in range(steps):
        mujoco.mj_step(m, d); xs.append(d.qpos[0])
    return np.array(xs), d.warning[mujoco.mjtWarning.mjWARN_BADQACC].number

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.1))
for h, col in ((0.002, "#2a9d5c"), (0.019, "#e8743b"), (0.0199, "#c0392b")):
    xs, bad = spring(h, steps=max(200, round(1.0 / h)))       # at least 1 s of simulated time
    ax.plot(np.arange(len(xs)) * h, xs * 100, lw=1.2, color=col, label=f"h = {h} s  (h·ω = {h*100:.2f})")
    print(f"h = {h:<6}  h*omega = {h*100:.2f}   largest |x| = {np.abs(xs).max()*100:5.2f} cm   BADQACC: {bad}")
for h in (0.0201, 0.021):
    xs, bad = spring(h)
    print(f"h = {h:<6}  h*omega = {h*100:.2f}   BADQACC: {bad}  -> MuJoCo gave up and reset x to {xs[-1]}")
x, v = 0.01, 0.0                                # explicit Euler, by hand, the "safe-looking" h = 0.002
for _ in range(500):
    x, v = x + 0.002 * v, v - 0.002 * 100**2 * x
print(f"explicit Euler by hand, h = 0.002, after 1 s: |x| = {abs(x)*100:,.0f} cm  (started at 1 cm)")
ax.set_xlim(0, 1.0); ax.set_xlabel("time (s)"); ax.set_ylabel("x (cm)"); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right", ncol=3); ax.set_ylim(-12, 16)
ax.set_title("released from 1 cm: the same spring at three timesteps (MuJoCo's Euler)", fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

---

## The bound, read {.smaller}

Each straight segment of the last figure is one step. The spring's period is
$2\pi/{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}$ = 0.063 s, so at ${\color{#c0392b}{h}}$ = 0.0199 s the simulator gets
barely 3 snapshots per oscillation — the "more than $\pi$ steps" rule, right at
its edge.

- **Green, ${\color{#c0392b}{h}}{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}} = 0.2$:** a clean 1 cm oscillation, 16 Hz — what the physics says.
- **Below the bound but close:** bounded, yet wrong — at ${\color{#c0392b}{h}}{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}} = 1.9$ a 1 cm
  release swings to 3.2 cm, at 1.99 to 10 cm. **Stable is not the same as accurate.**
- **Past 2.00:** it explodes within a few steps, MuJoCo raises `BADQACC` and
  resets the state to zero — which reads like a spring resting where it should.
- **Explicit Euler by hand, even at the safe-looking 0.002 s:** the 1 cm swing
  has grown to tens of metres after 1 s, as Step 3 promised.

---

## Damping moves the bound — in both directions {.smaller}

Real servos damp: ${\color{#e8743b}{\tau}} = -k\,x - c\,v$, with damping ratio
$\zeta = c / (2\sqrt{km})$ ($\zeta = 1$ is what `dampratio="1"` asks for). The
integrator can use the damper's force at the **old** velocity or at the **new** one:

| integrator | damper uses | step is stable when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Euler` (MuJoCo's default) | old $v_n$ (explicit) | ${\color{#c0392b}{h}}{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}} < 2\big(\sqrt{1+\zeta^2} - \zeta\big)$ |
| `implicitfast` (the G1's) | new $v_{n+1}$ (implicit) | ${\color{#c0392b}{h}}{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}} < 2\big(\sqrt{1+\zeta^2} + \zeta\big)$ |

**Where they come from** — the same three moves as before. **(a)** Write one step
as a 2 × 2 matrix. **(b)** Compute its determinant and trace: explicit damping
gives $\det A = 1 - 2\zeta{\color{#c0392b}{h}}{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}$ and
$\operatorname{tr}A = 2 - {\color{#c0392b}{h}}^2{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}^2 - 2\zeta{\color{#c0392b}{h}}{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}$.
**(c)** A 2 × 2 step is stable when $|\det A| < 1$ and $|\operatorname{tr}A| < 1 + \det A$;
the second rule is the quadratic $({\color{#c0392b}{h}}{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}})^2 + 4\zeta\,{\color{#c0392b}{h}}{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}} - 4 < 0$, whose positive root is the table's
first row. Implicit damping flips the sign of the $\zeta$ term (exercise 17).

```{python}
for z in (0.0, 1.0, 2.0):
    print(f"zeta = {z:.1f}:   Euler  h*omega < {2*(np.sqrt(1+z*z)-z):.3f}"
          f"     implicitfast  h*omega < {2*(np.sqrt(1+z*z)+z):.3f}")
```

With no damping both are the $2/{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}$ of the last slide. **An
explicitly computed damper makes the stiff spring *less* stable** — at
$\zeta = 1$ the safe step shrinks from $2/{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}$ to $0.83/{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}$ — while
computing it at the new velocity makes it *more* stable, to $4.83/{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}$.

---

## Our leg at h = 0.02 s: predict, then measure {.smaller}

Two joints push on each other through $M$, so the leg does not have "a hip
$\omega$" and "a knee $\omega$". It has two **modes** — patterns in which
both joints swing together — found from $K\boldsymbol\phi = {\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}}^2 M \boldsymbol\phi$:

```{python}
d0 = mujoco.MjData(leg); d0.qpos[:] = TARGET; mujoco.mj_forward(leg, d0)
M_leg = np.zeros((2, 2)); mujoco.mj_fullM(leg, d0, M_leg)
K_leg = np.diag(leg.actuator_gainprm[:, 0]); C_leg = np.diag(-leg.actuator_biasprm[:, 2])
L = np.linalg.cholesky(M_leg); Li = np.linalg.inv(L)       # K phi = w^2 M phi, made symmetric
w2, y = np.linalg.eigh(Li @ K_leg @ Li.T); modes = Li.T @ y
limit = []
for i in range(2):
    phi = modes[:, i]
    w = np.sqrt(w2[i]); z = (phi @ C_leg @ phi) / (2 * np.sqrt((phi @ K_leg @ phi) * (phi @ M_leg @ phi)))
    limit.append(2 * (np.sqrt(1 + z * z) - z) / w)
    print(f"mode {i}: shape (hip, knee) = {np.round(phi / np.abs(phi).max(), 2)}   "
          f"omega = {w:5.1f} rad/s   zeta = {z:.2f}   Euler needs h < {limit[-1]:.4f} s")
print(f"prediction: Euler is stable only below h = {min(limit):.4f} s\n")

for integ in ("Euler", "implicitfast"):
    for h in (0.002, 0.009, 0.0095, 0.015, 0.02):
        m = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string(LEG.replace('timestep="0.002"', f'timestep="{h}" integrator="{integ}"'))
        d = mujoco.MjData(m); d.qpos[:] = TARGET; d.ctrl[:] = TARGET; fastest = 0.0
        while d.time < 3.0:
            mujoco.mj_step(m, d)
            if d.time > 2.0: fastest = max(fastest, np.abs(d.qvel).max())
        print(f"{integ:12s} h = {h:<6}  fastest joint in the last second: {fastest:6.2f} rad/s"
              f"   BADQACC: {d.warning[mujoco.mjtWarning.mjWARN_BADQACC].number}")
```

The fast mode is mostly knee, and coupling gives it more damping than the
`dampratio="1"` we asked for — which, with an explicit damper, *lowers* its
limit. Past the predicted limit, `Euler` first **chatters without any warning**
(the leg "holds" while vibrating at tens of rad/s), then at 0.02 s fails on the
first step and resets. `implicitfast` holds still at every step size tried.

---

## Why `g1.xml` says `implicitfast` {.smaller}

The same test on the G1 standing for 3 s. Its stiffest servo is where the least
mass sits on a 500 N·m/rad spring — estimated per joint as
${\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}} \approx \sqrt{k_p / M_{ii}}$, with $M_{ii}$ the diagonal of the mass matrix:

```{python}
d = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand"); mujoco.mj_forward(model, d)
M = np.zeros((model.nv, model.nv)); mujoco.mj_fullM(model, d, M)
dof = model.jnt_dofadr[model.actuator_trnid[:, 0]]
w_joint = np.sqrt(model.actuator_gainprm[:, 0] / M[dof, dof])
i = int(np.argmax(w_joint))
zeta_i = -model.actuator_biasprm[i, 2] / (2 * np.sqrt(model.actuator_gainprm[i, 0] * M[dof[i], dof[i]]))
print(f"stiffest servo: {mujoco.mj_id2name(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_ACTUATOR, i)}, "
      f"omega = {w_joint[i]:.0f} rad/s, zeta = {zeta_i:.2f};  Euler then needs h*omega < 0.83")
print(f"   h*omega at 0.002 s = {0.002 * w_joint[i]:.2f},   at 0.004 s = {0.004 * w_joint[i]:.2f}\n")

saved = (model.opt.timestep, model.opt.integrator)
for integ in (mujoco.mjtIntegrator.mjINT_EULER, mujoco.mjtIntegrator.mjINT_IMPLICITFAST):
    for h in (0.002, 0.004, 0.01):
        model.opt.timestep, model.opt.integrator = h, integ
        d = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand")
        while d.time < 3.0:
            mujoco.mj_step(model, d)
        print(f"{integ.name[6:]:13s} h = {h:<6} pelvis height after 3 s: {d.qpos[2]:.3f} m")
model.opt.timestep, model.opt.integrator = saved      # put the G1 back exactly as loaded
```

At 500 Hz both integrators hold the robot — the stiffest servo sits at
${\color{#c0392b}{h}}{\color{#8e44ad}{\omega}} \approx 0.44$, inside even `Euler`'s 0.83. Double the step and
it crosses 0.83: `Euler` shakes the robot to the floor, `implicitfast` does not
notice. **The integrator line in the file is a safety margin**, and the formula
from two slides back predicted where it matters.

---

## Faster than real time {.smaller}

The whole argument for simulation is on this slide.

```{python}
import time

d = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand")
N = 5000
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(N):
    mujoco.mj_step(model, d)
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0

sim_seconds = N * model.opt.timestep
print(f"{N} steps in {elapsed:.2f} s of your life")
print(f"  = {N/elapsed:,.0f} physics steps per second")
print(f"  = {sim_seconds:.1f} s of robot time in {elapsed:.2f} s  ->  {sim_seconds/elapsed:.0f}x real time")
```

A 29-joint humanoid, tens of times faster than reality, on one core of whatever
machine you happen to be on. A real G1 falls over in real time, once, and then
needs repairing.

Hold on to your number. In week 10 you will want **150 million** steps, and this
is the figure that decides whether that takes an afternoon or a month.

## Watching it fall {.smaller}

Back to the G1, and do to it exactly what you just did to your own leg. We start
from the `<keyframe>` pose you read a few slides ago and **switch its motors
off**, then let physics run. (Week 0: `ctrl = 0` would *not* do this — the
position servos would hold a pose. To get no controller at all, actuation must be
disabled.)

```{python}
with soc4180.actuation_disabled(model):          # every servo dead
    data = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand")
    frames = soc4180.render_rollout(
        model, data, duration=3.0, fps=30, width=640, height=480
    )
soc4180.show_video(frames, fps=30)
```

---

## What you just saw

The robot collapsed. That is the correct result.

A humanoid is an **unstable** system: left alone it falls, exactly like a
broomstick balanced on your palm. Every remaining week of this course exists to
answer one question —

> what should the motors do, at each instant, so that it does not fall?

Weeks 2–6 answer it with mathematics. Weeks 7–15 answer it with learning.

---

## The numbers behind the video {.smaller}

Contacts are not declared anywhere in the MJCF. MuJoCo *finds* them, every step,
and you can read them.

```{python}
d = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand")     # servos on: the robot just stands
for _ in range(1000):
    mujoco.mj_step(model, d)

force = np.zeros(6)
total = 0.0
for i in range(d.ncon):
    mujoco.mj_contactForce(model, d, i, force)
    total += force[0]                          # normal component

print(f"contacts        : {d.ncon}")
print(f"sum of normals  : {total:.1f} N")
print(f"weight (m*g)    : {model.body_mass.sum() * 9.81:.1f} N")
```

**Eight contacts** — the four spheres under each foot, exactly the geoms you
found in the XML. And the ground pushes up with precisely the robot's weight,
because a standing robot is not accelerating. That is Newton's third law falling
out of the simulator, and it is the first thing to check when a robot misbehaves.

Week 4 lives entirely inside this number: to walk, you must move where those
contact forces act.

---

## Why the sum must equal the weight {.smaller}

**Step 1 — Newton, vertically, for the whole robot:**
$m\,\ddot z_{\text{CoM}} = \sum_i {\color{#e8743b}{F_{n,i}}} - m g$, where
${\color{#e8743b}{F_{n,i}}}$ is contact $i$'s push along the floor's normal (`force[0]`
from `mj_contactForce`, which reports each force in that contact's own frame
— normal first) and $z_{\text{CoM}}$ is the height of the centre of mass.

**Step 2 — standing still**, $\ddot z_{\text{CoM}} = 0$, so
$\sum_i {\color{#e8743b}{F_{n,i}}} = m g$ = 33.3 kg × 9.81 = 327.1 N. The motors cannot
change this sum: they push the robot against itself.

**Step 3 — no turning either**, so the forces' moments balance too: the
force-weighted average of the contact points (the **centre of pressure**, week 4)
must sit directly under the centre of mass.

The next slide checks both predictions against the eight contacts MuJoCo found.

---

## Where the 327 N lands, drawn {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
d = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand")
for _ in range(1000):
    mujoco.mj_step(model, d)
F, P = [], []
for i in range(d.ncon):
    mujoco.mj_contactForce(model, d, i, force); F.append(force[0]); P.append(d.contact[i].pos[:2].copy())
F, P = np.array(F), np.array(P)
cop = (F[:, None] * P).sum(0) / F.sum()
com = d.subtree_com[1][:2]                      # body 1 = pelvis: the whole robot hangs below it

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 3.6))
ax.scatter(P[:, 0], P[:, 1], s=F * 4, color="#e8743b", alpha=0.6, edgecolor="k")
for (x, y), f in zip(P, F):
    heel = x < 0
    ax.text(x + (-0.022 if heel else 0.022), y, f"{f:.0f} N", ha="right" if heel else "left",
            va="center", fontsize=8)
ax.plot(*cop, "x", color="#c0392b", ms=12, mew=2.5, label=f"centre of pressure  x = {cop[0]*1000:+.1f} mm")
ax.plot(*com, "o", mfc="none", mec="#3b7dd8", ms=14, mew=2, label=f"centre of mass       x = {com[0]*1000:+.1f} mm")
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlim(-0.14, 0.52); ax.set_ylim(-0.2, 0.2); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.set_xlabel("x forward (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("y left (m)"); ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="center right")
ax.set_title("the 8 foot spheres seen from above; disc area ∝ normal force", fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"sum = {F.sum():.1f} N;  heels (x < 0) carry {F[P[:,0] < 0].sum():.0f} N, toes {F[P[:,0] > 0].sum():.0f} N")
```

The heel spheres push about twice as hard as the toe spheres, because the
centre of mass is closer to the heels (heel spheres at $x = -5$ cm, toe
spheres at $+12$ cm, centre of mass at $+0.3$ cm) — and the centre of pressure lands under
it to a tenth of a millimetre, as Step 3 demands.

## Watching the floor push back {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
d = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand")
mujoco.mj_forward(model, d)                     # find the contacts at t = 0, before any step
print(f"at t = 0: {d.ncon} contacts, each sphere {-d.contact[0].dist * 1000:.2f} mm INTO the floor")
t, total, ncon = [], [], []
force = np.zeros(6)
while d.time < 1.0:
    mujoco.mj_step(model, d)
    s = 0.0
    for i in range(d.ncon):
        mujoco.mj_contactForce(model, d, i, force); s += force[0]
    t.append(d.time); total.append(s); ncon.append(d.ncon)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4, 3.2))
ax.plot(t, total, lw=1.5, color="#3b7dd8", label="sum of contact normal forces")
ax.axhline(model.body_mass.sum() * 9.81, color="k", ls="--", lw=1, label="weight $mg$")
ax.set_xlabel("time (s)"); ax.set_ylabel("N"); ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc="lower right"); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax2 = ax.twinx(); ax2.plot(t, ncon, color="#e8743b", lw=1, drawstyle="steps-post")
ax2.set_ylabel("contacts", color="#e8743b"); ax2.set_ylim(0, 10)
ax.set_title("the keyframe starts the feet slightly inside the floor; the floor pushes them out, then settles", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"largest push: {max(total):.0f} N at t = {t[int(np.argmax(total))]:.3f} s;  "
      f"after 0.5 s: {total[int(0.5 / model.opt.timestep)]:.1f} N;  weight {model.body_mass.sum() * 9.81:.1f} N")
```

The first tenth of a second is **not** a landing. The `stand` keyframe puts the
pelvis at 0.79 m, which leaves all eight foot spheres about 2 mm *inside* the
floor, so all eight contacts exist from the very first step (orange line, flat
at 8). MuJoCo's contacts are slightly soft — penetration makes force — so the
floor starts by pushing with well over the weight, pushes the robot up (the
pelvis *rises* in the one-step slide), undershoots once, and settles. From
about 0.15 s on, $\sum_i {\color{#e8743b}{F_{n,i}}} = mg$ to the decimal.

---

## Run it twice {.smaller}

```{python}
knee = model.jnt_qposadr[mujoco.mj_name2id(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_JOINT, "left_knee_joint")]

def fall(nudge=0.0, steps=1500):
    d = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand")
    d.qpos[knee] += nudge
    with soc4180.actuation_disabled(model):
        for _ in range(steps):
            mujoco.mj_step(model, d)
    return d.qpos.copy()

base = fall()
print(f"same run, twice        : max difference {np.abs(base - fall()).max():.1e}")
for nudge in (1e-12, 1e-9, 1e-6):
    diff = np.abs(base - fall(nudge)).max()
    print(f"knee nudged {nudge:.0e} rad : max difference {diff:.1e}   ({diff/nudge:,.0f}x bigger)")
```

Two facts, and they only *look* contradictory:

- **On one machine, the simulator is exactly deterministic** — the difference is
  a hard zero, not "small". Same input, same arithmetic, same answer.
- **A falling robot amplifies everything.** A knee nudge of $10^{-12}$ rad moves
  the foot about $3 \times 10^{-13}$ m — a fraction of an atom's width — and it
  grows five orders of magnitude in three seconds. At $10^{-6}$ rad the robot
  lands somewhere else entirely.

So the same code on a different machine gives a *different* fall — not through
randomness, but because the arithmetic is reordered. Ours settles at 0.134 m
here and 0.142 m on a Colab T4.

**Therefore, all semester: never assert an exact number from a fall, and never
grade one.** Assert direction and size — "dropped more than 0.5 m", "stayed above
0.7 m". A stable robot reproduces exactly; a falling one never will.

---

## The amplification, over time {.smaller}

Chaos has a signature: the gap between two nearby runs grows **exponentially**,
$\delta(t) \approx \delta_0\, e^{\lambda t}$, and $\lambda$ is a property of
the system, not of the nudge.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
def fall_trace(nudge, steps=1500):
    d = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand"); d.qpos[knee] += nudge; out = []
    with soc4180.actuation_disabled(model):
        for _ in range(steps):
            mujoco.mj_step(model, d); out.append(d.qpos.copy())
    return np.array(out)

ref = fall_trace(0.0)
tt = np.arange(1, 1501) * model.opt.timestep
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4, 3.4))
gaps = {}
for nudge, col in ((1e-12, "#3b7dd8"), (1e-9, "#2a9d5c"), (1e-6, "#e8743b")):
    gaps[nudge] = gap = np.abs(fall_trace(nudge) - ref).max(axis=1)
    ax.semilogy(tt, np.maximum(gap, 1e-17), lw=1.5, color=col, label=f"knee nudged {nudge:.0e} rad")
# fit the slope: a straight line through log(gap) against t, for the smallest nudge
# (from 0.2 s, past the first transient, to 3 s, while the gap is still small)
sel = (tt > 0.2) & (gaps[1e-12] > 0)
lam, logA = np.polyfit(tt[sel], np.log(gaps[1e-12][sel]), 1)
ax.semilogy(tt, np.exp(logA + lam * tt), ls=":", color="0.4", label=rf"fit: $\propto e^{{{lam:.1f}\,t}}$")
print(f"fitted growth rate lambda = {lam:.2f} per second  ->  x{np.exp(lam):.0f} per second, "
      f"x{np.exp(lam * 3):,.0f} over 3 s")
ax.set_xlabel("time (s)"); ax.set_ylabel("max |difference in qpos|"); ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which="both"); ax.set_title("three nudges, one slope: the slope is the robot's", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Reading a log axis:** a straight line means "the same factor every second".
The dotted line fits $\ln\delta = \ln\delta_0 + \lambda t$ to the blue curve:
$\lambda \approx 3.7$/s, i.e. $\times 40$ per second, $\times 7\times 10^{4}$ over
3 s — the five orders of magnitude *Run it twice* measured. The curves climb
roughly in parallel (the rate is the robot's, not the nudge's) until the gap is
as big as the robot: the orange one flattens near 1.

## Lab class: `mjcf_run.py` {.smaller}

```bash
uv run weeks/01-intro/mjcf_run.py --kp 20 --seconds 3
uv run weeks/01-intro/mjcf_run.py --timestep 0.02 --no-viewer
uv run weeks/01-intro/mjcf_run.py --xml my_robot.xml --target 0.5 0.5 0
```

The same leg, or any MJCF file, with `kp`, the timestep, the servos and
gravity as flags: compile → print → simulate → replay, in six numbered steps.

| Step | Does | Calls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | compile; apply the flags (`kv` rescaled with `kp`) | `MjModel.from_xml_string`, `opt.timestep`, `actuator_gainprm` |
| 2 | print what the compiler made | `jnt_qposadr`, `jnt_dofadr`, `mj_id2name` |
| 3 | put the leg at the target, command it | `jnt_qposadr[actuator_trnid]`, `ctrl` |
| 4 | the loop: a row of angles, droop, `BADQACC` per half second | `mj_step`, `data.warning` |
| 6 | replay the recorded motion | `launch_viewer(passive=True)`, `mj_forward`, `sync` |

1. Re-run the fall with `duration=6.0`. Where does the robot come to rest?
2. Print the joint **limits** (`model.jnt_range`). Which joints are unlimited, and why?
3. Set one hip joint to a non-zero angle in `data.qpos` before rendering. Does the
   robot fall differently?
4. `model.opt.gravity` holds the gravity vector. Set it to the Moon's
   $-1.62\ \text{m/s}^2$ and re-render. Does the robot fall more slowly than you
   expected?
5. `mjcf(g1_xml, "asset", limit=8)` lists the meshes. How many STL files does one
   humanoid need, and what does that say about where model-building effort
   actually goes?
6. The `foot` class sets `friction="0.6"`. Find it in `model.geom_friction`, then
   explain why only the *foot* spheres needed it and the elbow did not.
7. Set `left_hip_roll_joint` to 0.4 rad in `data.qpos`, run `mj_forward`, and
   render the pose. Which way did the leg go? Now do the same with
   `left_hip_yaw_joint`. Name each motion before you look.
8. Make two `MjData` from the one `model`. Step one 500 times and leave the other
   alone. Confirm `model` is unchanged and the two `data` disagree — this is the
   week-10 trick in miniature.
9. From your measured steps-per-second, work out how long week 10's **150 million**
   steps would take on this machine, in hours. Then read the week-10 title again.
10. Watch `data.ncon` during the fall — print it every 100 steps. When does it
    exceed 8, and which body has just hit the floor?
11. Re-run *Run it twice* with a **6 s** fall instead of 3 s. Does the
    amplification grow? Should it?

## Exercises: your own MJCF {.smaller}

12. Add `<freejoint/>` to `upper_leg` and re-compile. It refuses: *"more than 6
    dofs in body 'upper_leg'"*. A free joint **is** a body's entire freedom, so it
    cannot share a body with a hinge. Fix it by wrapping the leg in a parent body
    that carries the `<freejoint/>`, predict `nq` and `nv`, then re-render. What
    can the leg do now that it could not?
13. Sweep the servo gain — `kp` = 200, 100, 50, 20, 5 — and record the hip's droop
    from `TARGET`. Plot droop against `kp`. Does the error ever reach zero, and
    what would you have to add to the controller to make it?
14. Change `<option timestep="0.002"/>` to `0.02`. Re-run the **passive** swing:
    nothing crashes, nothing warns, and the final angles are simply different. Now
    re-run it **with the servos on** and inspect `data_leg.warning`. One of those
    two results is a silent approximation and the other is a silent failure —
    which is which, and which would have fooled you?
15. Add a third body, a foot, below `lower_leg`, with its own hinge. Confirm `nq`
    rose by one and that the foot moves when the knee does.
16. Replace the repeated `rgba` on the two capsules with a `<default>` class.
    Confirm the render is unchanged — this is the same mechanism that hides
    `kp=500` in the G1.
17. **Derive the `implicitfast` row.** With the damper at the new velocity,
    $v_{n+1} = v_n - h\omega^2 x_n - 2\zeta\omega h\, v_{n+1}$. Solve for
    $v_{n+1}$, write the step as a 2 × 2 matrix, and show
    $\det A = 1/(1 + 2\zeta h\omega)$. Then apply the rule
    $|\operatorname{tr}A| < 1 + \det A$ and recover
    $h\omega < 2(\sqrt{1+\zeta^2} + \zeta)$. Check your answer against the
    `implicitfast` column the slide printed.
18. In *The bound, measured*, change `kp="10000"` to `kp="40000"`. Predict the
    new largest safe step from $h < 2/\omega$ before you run it, then find it by
    bisection on `h`.
